newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices slip in India and Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices slip in India and Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton prices slipped in India and neighbouring Pakistan on rising supplies and weak demand, dealers in the two countries said on Thursday.
Dealers in Karachi said prices fell in the week to Thursday as international prices remained stable but demand for cotton yarn slumped before the Christmas and year-end holidays.
"A sharp fall in orders of cotton yarn from abroad due to holidays has slowed cotton buying by textile mills," dealer Iftikhar Ahmed of Lorica Pvt Ltd said.
An earlier buying spree ended after spinners retreated to the sidelines while ginners marked down rates to lure them back, said another dealer, Mustafa Hussain.
And fresh cotton arrivals from farms would depress prices further in the next few sessions, he added.
Dealers said high domestic prices had kept exporters out of the market while spinner-backed buying would soon slow down amid rising fresh arrivals.
In Pakistan's kerb market, NIAB-78 variety traded at 2,200 rupees ($54.69) per maund (37.32 kg) while MNH-93 was traded in the range of 2,290 and 2,125 rupees, the dealers said.

Thursday Wednesday Dec 12
In India, prices lost earlier gains on the local markets on improved arrivals and low mill demand last week, dealers said.

"Fresh buying by the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) petered out during the week while improved new crop supplies and sluggish mill demand dragged prices lower against earlier gains," one dealer said.
In spot deals, Bengal-deshi fell by 15/20 rupees to 820/860 rupees per maund while Punjab saw-ginned moved down by 10/60 rupees to 1,400/1,630 rupees per maund.
Punjab S-414 fell by 40/50 rupees to 1,840/1,860 rupees per maund. Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) fell to 17,800/18,200 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) from 18,000/18,600 rupees.
"New crop arrivals in the producing centres remained low earlier owing to cold weather but arrivals picked up later on," one broker said.
Daily arrivals in the Punjab region which had fallen to 18,000/20,000 bales (170 kg) later picked up to 25,000/30,000 bales.
"Traders were expecting fresh export quota from the Indian government but so far no confirmed announcement has been made in this direction," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading dealer.
"Earlier we were expecting a new crop of 17 million bales for the 1996/97 cotton season but now I am estimating the new crop to be barely 15.50 million bales," he said.
"Unseasonal rains as well as a cyclone in the producing centres had forced us to lower the crop estimate," he added.
"Sentiment remained subdued during the week but the market may look up again if government releases fresh export quota," one trader said.
The government has allowed exports of 600,000 bales so far this current season.
($1 = 40.22 Pakistan rupees)
